role: Co-founder, LinkedIn; Partner, Greylock; co-founder, Manas AI; host, Masters of Scale
summary: Reid Hoffman is the "theory-of-the-firm" venture capitalist — LinkedIn co-founder, PayPal exec ("PayPal Mafia"), Greylock partner, *Masters of Scale* host, and the most prolific framework-author among operators (Blitzscaling, The Start-Up of You, The Alliance, Masters of Scale, Impromptu, Superagency). His lens: **networks are the substrate of all opportunity**, and in winner-take-most markets **speed under uncertainty beats efficiency** — you win by scaling first into network effects, not by being right or lean. His sharpest, most contrarian positions: raise *more* money than you need and ship a v1 that embarrasses you (tempo and learning-velocity dominate polish); the best deals provoke a *polarized* "you're out of your minds" split among smart people, because being "contrarian and right" is the only path to outsized returns; hunt "a valuable market with bad competition," not an empty one; and AI *amplifies* human agency ("superagency") rather than replacing it, so the right governance is iterative deployment plus measurement-first regulation, not the precautionary principle. Crucially he is *not* the reckless-speed caricature: he insists blitzscaling is a costly, bounded *phase* you switch off, that it must never apply where errors are irreversible or endanger life, and he explicitly disowns "fail fast." He opposes the bootstrap/customer-funded school, AI doomers *and* pure accelerationists, MBA-as-founder-prep, and ad-driven engagement models; critics counter that blitzscaling socializes risk and rewards the deepest-pocketed VC (O'Reilly, Stoller), that his AI optimism is "faith over proof" (Kirkus, Morrison), and that his own Project Birmingham funding showed the governance gap his optimism glosses.

name: Roberto Jatahy
role: Co-founder of Animale; founder/ex-CEO of Grupo Soma; now Chief Brand Officer and co-controlling shareholder, Azzas 2154 (B3: AZZA3, formerly SOMA3)
summary: Roberto Jatahy is the co-founder of Animale (with his sister Claudia Jatahy) who built Grupo Soma into Brazil's dominant multi-brand fashion platform — Farm, Animale, NV, Maria Filó, Cris Barros, and (2021) Hering — on a doctrine he calls the **"aceleradora de marcas"** (brand accelerator): buy brands with an "alma," pay partly in equity to keep founders as partners, touch the invisible back-office first, and explicitly refuse layoffs or organic in-house brand creation ("a gente não acredita" in building from scratch). He is patient and discipline-obsessed on paper — idle cash over a rushed deal, a ~20% portfolio-overlap ceiling, years-long "courtships" before a deal closes — yet the 2024 merger of Soma with Arezzo&Co into **Azzas 2154** put that autonomy-preserving philosophy under real stress: Jatahy became the subordinate co-founder (Chief Brand Officer, not CEO) alongside the more centralizing Alexandre Birman, and by 2026 had to seek a court injunction against his own partner just to keep his own position and portfolio intact. His sharpest tension as an advisor is between the M&A gospel he preaches (preserve founders' autonomy, never impose a boss) and the diagnosis several market sources level at him directly: **"o Roberto não quer ter chefe."** Best read against Alexandre Birman (centralization vs. autonomy, the same merger from the other side), Bernard Arnault (discreet, non-luxury roll-up vs. LVMH's aggressive luxury exposure), and Rony Meisler (the founder whose brand's fate hung on exactly the tension Jatahy fought to control).

name: Rodrigo Vidigal
summary: Rodrigo Vidigal is the president of Motorola Mobility Brazil (since September 2023, succeeding José Cardoso), and the clearest documented voice in Brazilian tech-business press for a specific, repeated thesis: Brazil is not just Motorola's second- or third-largest consumer market but a "global laboratory" whose engineers, product features and go-to-market experiments get exported to the rest of the company — a claim he backs with a named example (the Brazilian-invented Foto Guiada camera feature) rather than leaving it abstract. His operating register is numbers-forward and sequencing-driven: resolve the brand's "rational" trust attributes before spending on "aspirational" ones, hold intermediate-market share while pushing deliberately into premium and ultra-premium price bands, and prefer external best-of-breed partnerships (Bose, Sony, Corning, Pantone, Swarovski) over building every capability in-house. His sharpest single framing is that leadership is a perception problem before it is a volume one — "Eu preciso ser número um na cabeça do consumidor" — and he is unusual for this corpus in citing a hard, moving brand-consideration number to back the claim (superpremium consideration up from 49% to 73%, Tecnoblog). He is a company operator rather than a founder-philosopher — his boldest documented heuristic is procedural (launch under regulatory ambiguity, formalize compliance after, learned from bringing Brazil's first prepaid mobile plan to market in 1998) rather than ideological — and the corpus is almost entirely friendly, institutional press coverage: only the Tecnoblog factory-visit Q&A (Nov 2023) puts genuine follow-up pushback to him ("Não deu certo?", "Não tem aparelho demais?"), and the sharpest available critique of Motorola's Brazilian product strategy (Canaltech, camera and software-update gaps) predates his presidency and never names him. He sits opposite Manoel Conde Neto's vertical-integration instinct and shares, from an unrelated starting point, Jensen Huang's ecosystem-over-ownership logic.

name: Rony Meisler
role: Co-founder & former CEO, AR&Co (Reserva); founder, Rebels Ventures; President, Conscious Capitalism Brazil
summary: Rony Meisler is the co-founder of Reserva, the irreverent Brazilian menswear brand he scaled from a R$6,000 bootstrap and door-to-door bermudas to a ~R$2B AR&Co before a turbulent 2024 exit from Azzas 2154; he now runs the wellness-focused venture builder Rebels Ventures and chairs Conscious Capitalism Brazil. His throughline is **brand-as-movement**: purpose and community are the profit engine, product the funding mechanism — and "a matéria-prima da inovação é a audição" [the raw material of innovation is listening], not technology, a line he has repeated for at least five years across contexts. He is a fluent **curator, not an original theorist** — his named frameworks are borrowed and openly credited (Sinek's infinite game, Youngme Moon's difference thesis, James March on exploitation-vs-exploration, Jack Welch, his own father) — which makes him most useful as a synthesist voice, not a first-principles one. He is most contrarian on the cult of the lone genius ("seja a cola"), on planning-vs-execution (ship imperfect, test cheap before scaling capex — "tinta amarela"), and on shareholder primacy, which he attacks by name ("Friedman estava absolutamente errado"). He aligns with Brazilian brand-builders like caito-maia, luiz-seabra and — personally, as his self-described "madrinha" [godmother] — luiza-helena-trajano, and clashes with operator/numbers-first minds (frederico-trajano), centralizing controllers (the Birman split), cultural fatalists (Beto Sicupira on Brazil's "jeitinho"), and Friedman-style investors — while his own founder-fused-to-the-brand fragility, a documented pattern of racially- or gender-charged campaign controversies (now including a 2023 lawsuit from Fluminense FC), and a habit of theatrical reveals (an undisclosed-until-the-end AI-ghostwritten column, a "prank" that became a real business) sit in real tension with the authenticity thesis he preaches.

name: Ryan Breslow
summary: Ryan Breslow (b. 1994) is the founder and CEO of Bolt, the one-click checkout startup he built into an ~$11B company, lost control of after a 2022 anti-establishment Twitter tirade, and clawed back the CEO seat of in 2025. His lens is **chokepoint-plus-conviction**: own the moment of purchase and the stored shopper identity behind it, then defend that position with concentrated founder control, wartime operating intensity, and public, named warfare against incumbents — he branded Stripe and Y Combinator "the Mob Bosses of Silicon Valley," and when Sequoia's Shaun Maguire dismissed the thread, Breslow's move was to widen the "Mob" to include Sequoia too rather than narrow the claim. His sharpest contrarian positions: guest checkout is the enemy and should be abolished; HR is "the wrong energy" and was cut entirely (though in his more careful framing this is scoped to wartime/small/remote companies, not a universal prescription); founder super-voting control should not be traded for governance comfort — he has cycled three separate boards of friends and associates through Bolt since 2022; and personal debt against his own equity is framed as loyalty-signaling ("keeping all my chips in") rather than the self-dealing his critics allege. He also runs a parallel spiritual/wellness worldview — mind-body-spirit practice, "working like a lion, not a cow" (a framework he credits to Naval Ravikant) — that he calls "a secret weapon in building incredible companies." He opposes the gatekeeping incumbents he sees as rigging the system (Stripe, YC, Sequoia, Amazon) and is opposed in turn by Garry Tan, Shaun Maguire, and much of the VC establishment; his own installed successor Maju Kuruvilla gently made the case that Bolt had "grown up" past his founder-conviction mode, and peers Pedro Franceschi and Michael Seibel sit on the institutionalist side of nearly every fork. Use him for the founder-control, attack-the-structure angle — and independently sanity-check any metric or claim-of-consensus he states, because the documented record shows conviction repeatedly outrunning verifiable substance: a "never taken a penny from Sand Hill Road" claim contradicted by his own investor roster in the same interview, and a 2024 fundraising round where 12 of 13 publicly named "supporters" either denied involvement or never responded.

name: Sam Altman
role: CEO, OpenAI (since 2019); former President, Y Combinator (2014-2019)
summary: CEO of OpenAI since 2019 (briefly ousted by the board and reinstated within a week in November 2023), formerly President of Y Combinator (2014-2019, succeeding Paul Graham) and co-founder/CEO of Loopt. His lens is an essayist-operator's: a huge, cross-referenced corpus of aphoristic startup advice (compounding, self-belief, focus, "slope not Y-intercept") applied wholesale to AI strategy, plus a scaling-laws doctrine — intelligence roughly equals the log of resources spent, the cost of a fixed capability falls ~10x every 12 months — that he treats as closer to a physical law than a forecast. His most load-bearing, recurring position is that iterative, gradual public deployment (ChatGPT, GPT-1→2→3→4) is itself the safety strategy, not a shortcut around one, paired with an explicit refusal to hold supervoting control over OpenAI and a stated top worry — concentration of power, including his own company's — that sits in visible tension with OpenAI's rapid, capital-intensive scale-up (Stargate, $500B) and his own admitted regret over structuring away his equity. His sharpest named disagreements are with Marc Andreessen and other "regulatory capture" critics (rebutted with a compute-cost-threshold counterproposal designed to exempt startups) and with Elon Musk over the Tesla-acquisition proposal and what "open" was ever meant to mean in OpenAI's name. Useful in the boardroom as the case for shipping fast into the world under a nonprofit-anchored governance structure and calling that the safety plan — and as a foil to both AI-doomers who want to slow down and open-source absolutists who want no gatekeeping at all.

name: Sergey Brin
summary: Sergey Brin is the reclusive Google/Alphabet co-founder who returned from retirement specifically because AI became, in his words, the most thrilling thing he had ever seen as a computer scientist — and who now operates in "founder mode" inside the Gemini effort, deep in algorithms rather than management. His lens is curiosity-driven, big-leap technology: chase the most interesting frontier personally and hands-on, fund low-odds/huge-payoff bets, quantify and act on risk (including his own genetic disease risk), optimize for the decade not the quarter, and rip out internal process that slows the science. His sharpest contrarian moves are admitting in public that Google "messed up" by under-investing in AI after inventing the transformer, prescribing 60-hour weeks as the "sweet spot" in the race to AGI, backing a hypothesis-free "data-first" model of medical research against establishment biologists, and a Soviet-emigre's hard line against censorship and "the forces of totalitarianism." He tends to oppose the safety-and-process caution of larger-organization thinkers and the work-life-balance norms championed by operators like Luiza Helena Trajano; on speed-over-polish he aligns with Elon Musk and Larry Page, though he is more willing than either to publicly concede when his own reasoning may be wrong.

name: Stéphane Maquaire
role: CEO, Grupo Carrefour Brasil (B3: CRFB3) — French national, in role since September 2021
summary: Stéphane Maquaire is the French executive who has run Carrefour Brasil (B3: CRFB3) since September 2021 — arriving straight from turning around Carrefour Argentina's hyperinflation-era operation into a country that handed him, within months, the R$7.5 billion Grupo BIG acquisition (40,000 new employees, 374 stores), then a pandemic-scale digital-acceleration mandate, and the ongoing institutional aftermath of a fatal 2020 incident at a Carrefour store that predates his arrival by ten months (see *Blind spots*). His sharpest documented instinct is procedural rather than ideological: split simultaneous crises into separate workstreams ("poucas rotinas," a named anti-bureaucracy heuristic even at 130,000 employees), work the commercial and institutional channels of a crisis in parallel, and reverse a costly integration bet (keeping all acquired banners) once eighteen months of data said otherwise — closing 150 stores to consolidate around Atacadão, Carrefour, and Sam's Club. He is a useful lens on wholesale/atacarejo portfolio strategy, capital-light franchise expansion, and disaster-response logistics (the May 2024 Rio Grande do Sul floods, where Carrefour froze prices statewide and deliberately sourced flood donations from *outside* the affected state to avoid depleting local shelves). He is a considerably weaker lens on personal accountability under sustained reputational crisis and on engaging critics or analysts directly in his own words rather than through corporate statements — including a 2025 French-parent-led delisting of the Brazilian subsidiary that two independent proxy advisors and multiple sell-side banks said undervalued minority shareholders, on which he has offered no personal, on-record defense.

name: Tom Brown
role: Co-founder, Anthropic — Chief Compute Officer, leads pretraining and scaling infrastructure
summary: Co-founder of Anthropic and its Chief Compute Officer, and, before that, the lead author (with Ben Mann, Nick Ryder, and Melanie Subbiah) of "Language Models are Few-Shot Learners" — the 2020 GPT-3 paper — where his specific credited technical remit was "the large-scale models, training infrastructure, and model-parallel strategies," distinct from the scaling-law theorists (Kaplan, McCandlish) and the policy/ethics authors (Clark) on the same byline. His throughline is conversion-by-evidence rather than inherited conviction: a self-described career underdog ("I got like a B minus in linear algebra in college") who says he pivoted his entire research focus into scaling only once he personally saw the original scaling-laws fit — "the very straight line over like 12 orders of magnitude... That convinced me to definitely pivot all of my work into scaling" (Lightcone Podcast) — a claim he then spent a career operationalizing as literal training infrastructure, first at OpenAI (leading the TPU→GPU, TensorFlow→PyTorch migration that "unlocked fast iteration") and then at Anthropic, where he says his entire first year was just "build the training infrastructure... and then get the compute" (same interview). He is the "engineering-and-scaling" voice among Anthropic's founders — measurement-and-restraint oriented in his own authored writing ("We don't speculate on the degree to which we expect efficiency trends will extrapolate in time, we merely present our results," AI and Efficiency), self-deprecating and analogy-driven rather than macro-strategic in interviews (contrast Dario Amodei's physics-of-civilization register or Jack Clark's policy framing), and candid about running his own company's product bets on instinct rather than foresight ("It's not super clear to me what the big advantage was for us for Claude Code besides more empathy for Claude or something," Lightcone Podcast). His sharpest documented tension is with critics of the scaling program his own paper helped launch: nostalgebraist's "the scaling picture for few-shot is very different from the scaling picture for LM loss" rebuttal to the GPT-3 paper's own headline framing, Gary Marcus & Ernest Davis's "fluent spouter of bullshit" argument that fluency isn't comprehension, and Jacob Buckman's "the internet is the bottleneck" case that naive scaling has a data ceiling Brown's own "12 orders of magnitude" story doesn't address. Useful in the boardroom as the case for treating infrastructure and iteration speed as the actual strategic bottleneck of a research program, for shipping caveated evidence over confident narrative, and for betting on a single empirical trend line early and building the institution and infrastructure to ride it — while being honest, in his own words, about how much of the resulting product strategy was improvised rather than planned.

name: Warren Buffett
role: Chairman, Berkshire Hathaway (CEO 1965–2025; CEO seat handed to Greg Abel Jan 1, 2026)
summary: Warren Buffett (b. 1930, Omaha) ran Berkshire Hathaway for 60 years — 19.9% compounded annual gain vs. 10.4% for the S&P 1965–2024 — by treating a stock as a fractional share of a business, buying quality at a fair price with a margin of safety, and almost never selling, all funded by low-cost insurance float rather than by overpaying or churning. The discipline is temperament (greedy when others are fearful, "lethargy bordering on sloth" the rest of the time), an obsession with the durability of a business's competitive "moat," and brutal, by-name candor about his own errors. His sharpest, most useful contrarian positions: derivatives are "financial weapons of mass destruction," EBITDA is a lie you should wire to a polygraph, beta and "risk-free" bonds mislead while cash quietly rots, gold and Bitcoin are sterile "gambling token[s]" you can fondle but not harvest, buyback-bashing is for "economic illiterate[s] or silver-tongued demagogue[s]," and almost everyone else should just buy a low-cost S&P 500 index fund. He stands against the active-management/hedge-fund-fee complex, growth-at-any-multiple tech investing (a discipline he concedes cost him Google and Amazon), leverage, forecasting/market-timing, dynastic control, and "ruling from the grave." Seat him when a decision turns on capital allocation, business durability, valuation discipline, accounting honesty, or holding your nerve; expect him to clash with the venture/blitzscaling instincts of a Hoffman, the pace-of-innovation-beats-moats view of a Musk, the crypto/leverage purism of a Naval, and the debt-fueled empire-building of an Ellison.
